comparison_other_segmenter.why: the two segmenters are run on identical notes and identical spans so the difference is attributed rather than guessed. It is a trade, not a win: our boundaries take the structural operators (header, lab-block, bullet, whitespace) toward zero because they model list and header structure, and lose badly on deid_restyle because they also model de-identification placeholders — so the placeholder convention is an input to their own rules. PyRuSH models neither, which is why restyling barely moves it and list structure moves it a lot.

how_to_read: zero is the only good answer. A non-zero flip rate is the size of a confound, not a performance number, and it bounds what an assertion-conditioned result can claim. Read the two segmenters per operator rather than on the overall figure: the overall numbers are close and their composition is completely different.
prior_finding: probe_deid_assertion.py found one instance on ONE note: three de-id conventions, including MIMIC-III's and MIMIC-IV's, merge two list items so a negation cue takes scope over the next. This is the same question at corpus scale over every invariant operator.
question: Does an assertion survive a perturbation proved not to change clinical reference?
why_these_operators: each declares a canonicalizer kappa and CI proves kappa(apply(d)) == kappa(d) over the corpus at every severity, so no clinical reference can change. A flip therefore means the assertion layer is reading something that is not clinical content, and every result conditioned on assertion inherits it as a confound.
